reason:
The artifact contains only kernel.py, meta.json and problem.txt — no test.py or get_inputs — so problem.txt is the operative contract, and it explicitly requires (a) sorted_keys[n,:] non-decreasing and (b) a STABLE tie rule ("the one with the LOWER original index must come first"), with duplicate keys declared expected in the input domain because the keys are quantized scores. Two confirmed in_scope claims show the kernel does not implement those required behaviors.

c1 (confirmed, t9): the comparator at line 41 uses (keys == p_key) & (perm > p_perm), declaring the tied entry with the LARGER original index smaller. Runtime evidence at power-of-two W (so the padding path cannot confound it): all-equal row W=8 returned perm=[7,6,5,4,3,2,1,0] versus the stable reference [0..7]; across W in {8,16,32,64} with keys in [0,4), 64/64 rows had perm != torch.sort(stable=True).indices while sorted_keys matched torch.sort values in 64/64 rows; 8/8 rows matched an explicitly anti-stable reference. This is systematic descending-index tie-breaking, not nondeterminism and not an unspecified tie choice — problem.txt fixes the tie order and ties it to which memory slot is read.

c2 (confirmed, t10): every compare-exchange against a padding lane is skipped because both branches of should_take_partner are gated by (partner < W) (lines 43-44) instead of the real lane receiving a +INF sentinel, so the bitonic network is invalid for non-power-of-two W. With distinct keys (no ties to confound), non-monotonic rows out of 32 were W=3:20, W=5:24, W=6:31, W=7:32, W=9:31, W=12:32, W=100:32 (e.g. keys=[3,1,2] -> [1,3,2]), while power-of-two controls {4,8,16,64} had 0 failures. problem.txt states the input is [N,W] int64 with no power-of-two restriction, so these widths are inside the stated domain and the required monotonicity applies.

c3 was rebutted: the gather identity sorted_keys[n,i]==keys[n,perm[n,i]] held 0/64 failures at every width up to BLOCK_W=1024, perm was always a valid permutation, and results were bit-identical over 3 runs, so the write-after-read hazard is a latent source note only under the shipped num_warps=1. That rebuttal does not weaken c1/c2 — it is precisely why consistency-only checks miss them. No unresolved claim is being set aside; c1 and c2 are each independently sufficient for reject.
